title: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: Inspired by the superior language abilities of large language models (LLM), large vision-language models (LVLM) have been recently proposed by integrating powerful LLMs for improving the performance on complex multimodal tasks. Despite the promising progress on LVLMs, we find that they suffer from object hallucinations, i.e., they tend to generate objects inconsistent with the target images in the descriptions. To investigate it, this work presents the first systematic study on object hallucination of LVLMs. We conduct the evaluation experiments on several representative LVLMs, and show that they mostly suffer from severe object hallucination issues. We further discuss that the visual instructions may influence the hallucination, and find that: objects that frequently appear in the visual instructions or co-occur with the image objects are obviously prone to be hallucinated by LVLMs. Besides, we further design a polling-based query method called POPE for better evaluation of object hallucination. Experiment results show that our POPE can evaluate object hallucination in a more stable and flexible way.

claims.text: Most instruction-tuned Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) severely suffer from object hallucination issues.
Objects that frequently appear in visual instruction datasets are prone to be hallucinated by LVLMs.
Objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth image objects are prone to be hallucinated by LVLMs.
POPE formulates the evaluation of object hallucination as a binary Yes/No classification task.
InstructBLIP achieves an F1 score of 89.29 under the POPE Random sampling setting on the MSCOCO validation dataset.
LLaVA achieves an F1 score of 68.65 under the POPE Random sampling setting on the MSCOCO validation dataset.
LVLM evaluation performance consistently drops across all tested models when transitioning from Random to Popular and Adversarial sampling settings in POPE.
POPE metrics exhibit lower standard deviation across prompt template variations compared to the CHAIR metric.
The degree of object hallucination in an LVLM is not always consistent with its Visual Question Answering (VQA) task performance.

limitations.text: The CHAIR metric is unstable across different prompt instructions and relies on complex human-crafted exact-matching parsing rules that misclassify generated text styles.
The evaluation focuses only on coarse object-level hallucinations and does not consider fine-grained attributes, positions, or quantities of objects.
Evaluation was conducted on a subset of the validation split due to computational resource constraints.
Matching-based answer parsing in POPE can fail when LVLMs occasionally produce responses that do not explicitly contain 'Yes' or 'No'.
When combined with automatic segmentation tools like SEEM, object label sets may diverge from human ground-truth annotations, leading to evaluation result differences.

future_work.text: Evaluating fine-grained object hallucinations, including object numbers, attributes, and spatial positions.
Extending POPE evaluation to a larger selection of recent open-source and closed-source LVLMs.

methodologies.name: Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation (POPE)
methodologies.description: A polling method that converts object hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task probing target images with Yes/No questions using Random, Popular, and Adversarial negative sampling strategies.
